Plenty of headroom (1.6 TB free), `x86_64-linux-gnu`. And noted on `correctness-performance.md` — that's a separate track (tic-tac-toe / language-correctness + interpreter-perf), now closed; it isn't part of the CUDA pivot, so I'll leave it.

Here's what I found and what I propose.

## Where the GPU story stands

The **MLX track is effectively done** (saga `local-gpu-agentic`, steps 004–010): forward + backward + Adam all run on the Apple GPU, and the "MLX LoRA fine-tune" demo is relabeled true-GPU. The architecture it left behind is the template a CUDA track slots into:

| MLX crate | Role | CUDA analog to build |
|---|---|---|
| `mlpl-mlx-rt` | forward ops (`mlx_rs::Array`) | `mlpl-cuda-rt` |
| `mlpl-mlx-forward` | embed / rms_norm / attention / cross-entropy | `mlpl-cuda-forward` |
| `mlpl-mlx-train` | `value_and_grad` + `MlxAdam` (on-device) | `mlpl-cuda-train` |
| `mlpl-mlx-model` | `demo_forward` assembly | `mlpl-cuda-model` |
| `mlpl-mlx-serve` | server-side peer dispatcher | `mlpl-cuda-serve` |

The plumbing is **already CUDA-aware**: `Device::Cuda` exists in the demo registry (rendered visible-but-not-runnable), `Value::DeviceTensor` carries a `device: String` with `"cuda"` called out in comments, and `device("cuda") { … }` already parses and pushes onto the device stack — it just falls back to CPU because no `cuda` dispatch exists. The MLX dispatch in `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` is the one place to generalize.

## The decisive advantage of pivoting now

This box is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA 13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, 1.6 TB free.** Unlike the MLX track — which this Linux machine can never build or test — **a CUDA track is fully buildable and testable right here, in-session.** TDD with real GPU parity tests, not Apple-only glue I can't run.

## The MLX demos to mirror

4 demo scripts (`lora_finetune_mlx`, `tiny_lm_mlx`, `neural_thicket_mlx`, `mlx_remote`) and 2 headline literate **org docs** (`examples/literate/mlx-lora-finetune.org`, `tictactoe-finetune.org` → rendered to `pages/literate/*.html`). "CUDA equivalent demo + org doc for each" maps cleanly onto those.

## Proposed first saga: `cuda-foundation`

Mirror the MLX foundation up to **one demo end-to-end with its org doc**, proven on this GPU — then repeat for the rest in a follow-up saga.

1. **`cuda-backend-spike`** — pick the CUDA backend crate and prove `value_and_grad` + Adam on *this* GPU with a tiny regression (direct analog of MLX step 005, the load-bearing decision/spike). De-risks Blackwell sm_120 / CUDA 13 support up front.
2. **`mlpl-cuda-rt`** — forward ops crate, gated `cfg(all(feature="cuda", target_os="linux"))`, parity-tested vs CPU.
3. **`cuda-dispatch-wire`** — generalize `try_mlx_dispatch`/`dispatched_call` so `device("cuda")` routes through `mlpl-cuda-rt`; CPU fallback + one-time warning preserved.
4. **`cuda-forward-primitives` + `cuda-model`** — embed/rms_norm/attention/cross-entropy + `demo_forward`, parity vs CPU.
5. **`cuda-lora-demo`** — first CUDA demo (`lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl`) end-to-end via `eval_adam`'s CUDA branch + its `.org` literate doc; registry entry flips to runnable on a connected CUDA peer.
6. **`cuda-connect-peer`** — `mlpl-cuda-serve` so `mlpl-serve --features cuda` on Linux is a connect-mode peer, and a `GET /api/devices` capability probe so the UI knows whether a connected server offers `mlx`, `cuda`, or neither (this is what makes "connect to a Mac and/or this Arch box" honest gating instead of a static guess).

I want to confirm three load-bearing decisions before I start the spike, since they shape every step:

=== agentic-ask-plan.md ===
# Agentic `:ask` -- Saga Plan (tool-using, RLM-like)

## Vision

Today `:ask` sends one context-rich prompt to Ollama. The goal is
to make it **agent-like**: a tool-capable model is given a *meta
context* describing what context is *available on request*, and it
**requests** only what it needs (recent history, a variable's
shape/values, the selected sculpture, a builtin's help, a demo's
source) via tool calls, then answers from what it retrieved. This
is the start of Recursive-Language-Model-style tooling -- the model
drives a retrieval/answer loop instead of being flooded up front.

## Already shipped (the foundation this builds on)

- **Connect-mode evaluator swap (SSE).** `?connect=<url>` routes
  REPL eval to `mlpl-serve`, executed server-side (no browser CORS,
  no WASM `std::time` panic). `connect.rs` + `eval_wasm::connect_eval`.
- **Contextual `:ask`.** Prompt = a "you are inside the sw-MLPL
  REPL" system preamble + recent REPL activity + the selected 3D
  sculpture summary (`window.__stage3d_context()`). Plus `:history`,
  the in-dialog **Ask** button (`window.__mlpl_ask`), and
  configurable `?ollama=` / `?model=`.
- **Ollama tool-calling verified.** Capable models (`llama3.1`,
  `qwen2.5-coder:14b`) return proper `tool_calls`; the tiny
  `qwen2.5:0.5b` emits the call as plain text -- so the agent loop
  needs a strong model (e.g. `qwen2.5-coder:14b` on the LAN box).

## Phase 0 -- Ollama settings exposure (prerequisite)

Make host + model first-class and discoverable rather than
hard-coded / query-string-only:

- **Host:** `localhost:11434` or a LAN host (e.g.
  `http://large12:11434`). The call is server-side, so any host
  reachable from `mlpl-serve` works.
- **Server-owned config:** a `config.toml` (and/or CLI flags /
  `OLLAMA_HOST` env) on `mlpl-serve` holding the default host +
  default model, so the browser carries nothing.
- **List models:** `GET <host>/api/tags` -> a model picker in the
  UI; a `:models ollama` listing (distinct from MLPL `:models`).
- **Default + override:** choose a default model; override per call
  (`:ask --model qwen2.5-coder:14b <question>` and/or a UI
  dropdown). Replaces the current `?ollama=`/`?model=` stopgap.

## Phase 1 -- proper system/user messages

Switch from `/api/generate` with the system text embedded in the
prompt to `/api/chat` with a real `system` message + `user`
message (Ollama supports both). Weak models follow a real system
role far better. Extend `llm_call` (optional `system` arg) or add a
server-side `ask()` builtin.

## Phase 2 -- the tool-using agent loop

Run the loop **server-side** (it owns the live session):

1. `POST <host>/api/chat` with `messages` + `tools` (function defs)
   + the meta-context system prompt ("you have these tools; request
   only what you need; do not guess").
2. If the reply has `tool_calls`, fulfill each from the session and
   append the results as `tool` messages; loop (bounded depth /
   token budget).
3. When the model returns content with no tool calls, that's the
   answer.

**Context-provider tools** (map to existing introspection):

| tool | source |
|------|--------|
| `get_recent_history()` | REPL history (client snapshot) |
| `get_workspace_vars()` | session env (`:vars`) |
| `describe_variable(name)` | `:describe` / inspect |
| `get_selected_sculpture()` | client `__stage3d_context()` snapshot |
| `get_builtin_help(name)` | `:help` table |
| `get_demo_source(name)` | the demo registry |

Client-only context (the 3D selection) is passed as a snapshot in
the initial request so the server can answer those tool calls
without a round-trip to the browser. Surface the tool-call trace in
the UI for transparency ("the model looked at: history, var X").

## Phase 3 -- the RLM demo

A demo that **runs ML steps, then asks for help**:

1. Train a tiny model (or build an attention pattern) -- a few REPL
   lines.
2. Issue an agentic `:ask` ("why did the loss plateau?" / "what does
   this attention pattern show, given my setup?").
3. The model calls `get_recent_history` + `get_workspace_vars` +
   `describe_variable`, then answers from what it retrieved -- the
   visible RLM-like loop.

## Open questions / decisions

- **Model requirement:** tool-capable; default to a strong remote
  one (`qwen2.5-coder:14b` on `large12`). Document the floor.
- **Where the loop lives:** server-side; client passes the 3D
  selection snapshot. (A future variant could let the server call
  back to the client for live UI state.)
- **Flooding control:** per-tool result size caps; the point of the
  meta-context is selective retrieval.
- **Security:** the server makes outbound calls -- allow-list the
  Ollama host(s) in config (mirrors the connect-mode CORS
  allow-list).
- **Live-demo gating:** these features only work in connect mode;
  the GitHub Pages demo should mark them visible-but-not-runnable
  (a `requires_connect` flag on the demo registry -- separate small
  task).

## References

- `docs/using-ollama.md`, `docs/using-cli-server.md` -- LLM + server.
- `components/web-handlers/.../connect.rs` -- current `:ask`.
- `components/runtime-core/.../llm_builtins.rs` -- `call_ollama`.
- Recursive Language Models (external research) -- the inspiration.

  `qwen2.5:0.5b` emits the call as plain text -- so the agent loop
  needs a strong model (e.g. `qwen2.5-coder:14b` on the LAN box).

## Phase 0 -- Ollama settings exposure (prerequisite)

Make host + model first-class and discoverable rather than
hard-coded / query-string-only:

- **Host:** `localhost:11434` or a LAN host (e.g.
  `http://large12:11434`). The call is server-side, so any host
  reachable from `mlpl-serve` works.
- **Server-owned config:** a `config.toml` (and/or CLI flags /
  `OLLAMA_HOST` env) on `mlpl-serve` holding the default host +
  default model, so the browser carries nothing.
- **List models:** `GET <host>/api/tags` -> a model picker in the
  UI; a `:models ollama` listing (distinct from MLPL `:models`).
- **Default + override:** choose a default model; override per call
  (`:ask --model qwen2.5-coder:14b <question>` and/or a UI
  dropdown). Replaces the current `?ollama=`/`?model=` stopgap.

## Phase 1 -- proper system/user messages

Switch from `/api/generate` with the system text embedded in the
prompt to `/api/chat` with a real `system` message + `user`
message (Ollama supports both). Weak models follow a real system
role far better. Extend `llm_call` (optional `system` arg) or add a
server-side `ask()` builtin.

## Phase 2 -- the tool-using agent loop

Run the loop **server-side** (it owns the live session):

1. `POST <host>/api/chat` with `messages` + `tools` (function defs)
   + the meta-context system prompt ("you have these tools; request
   only what you need; do not guess").
2. If the reply has `tool_calls`, fulfill each from the session and
   append the results as `tool` messages; loop (bounded depth /
   token budget).
3. When the model returns content with no tool calls, that's the
   answer.

**Context-provider tools** (map to existing introspection):

| tool | source |
|------|--------|
| `get_recent_history()` | REPL history (client snapshot) |
| `get_workspace_vars()` | session env (`:vars`) |
| `describe_variable(name)` | `:describe` / inspect |
| `get_selected_sculpture()` | client `__stage3d_context()` snapshot |
| `get_builtin_help(name)` | `:help` table |
| `get_demo_source(name)` | the demo registry |

Client-only context (the 3D selection) is passed as a snapshot in
the initial request so the server can answer those tool calls
without a round-trip to the browser. Surface the tool-call trace in
the UI for transparency ("the model looked at: history, var X").

## Phase 3 -- the RLM demo

A demo that **runs ML steps, then asks for help**:

1. Train a tiny model (or build an attention pattern) -- a few REPL
   lines.
2. Issue an agentic `:ask` ("why did the loss plateau?" / "what does
   this attention pattern show, given my setup?").
3. The model calls `get_recent_history` + `get_workspace_vars` +
   `describe_variable`, then answers from what it retrieved -- the
   visible RLM-like loop.

## Open questions / decisions

- **Model requirement:** tool-capable; default to a strong remote
  one (`qwen2.5-coder:14b` on `large12`). Document the floor.
- **Where the loop lives:** server-side; client passes the 3D
  selection snapshot. (A future variant could let the server call
  back to the client for live UI state.)
- **Flooding control:** per-tool result size caps; the point of the
  meta-context is selective retrieval.
- **Security:** the server makes outbound calls -- allow-list the
  Ollama host(s) in config (mirrors the connect-mode CORS
  allow-list).
- **Live-demo gating:** these features only work in connect mode;
  the GitHub Pages demo should mark them visible-but-not-runnable
  (a `requires_connect` flag on the demo registry -- separate small
  task).

- `docs/using-ollama.md`, `docs/using-cli-server.md` -- LLM + server.
- `components/web-handlers/.../connect.rs` -- current `:ask`.
- `components/runtime-core/.../llm_builtins.rs` -- `call_ollama`.
- Recursive Language Models (external research) -- the inspiration.

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

This first saga is the **foundation + one demo end-to-end**, proven
on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Why now, why here

This dev host is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell, sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA
13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, x86_64-linux-gnu, 1.6 TB free**. Unlike the
MLX track -- which this Linux box can never build or test -- a CUDA
track is fully buildable and TDD-testable in-session with real GPU
parity tests, not Apple-only glue.

## Foundation already in place (CUDA-aware plumbing)

- **`Device::Cuda`** exists in the web-demos registry
  (`mlpl-web-demos-types`), rendered visible-but-not-runnable on the
  public live demo.
- **`Value::DeviceTensor { device: String, .. }`** already names
  `"cuda"` as a future device (`mlpl-eval-types`).
- **`device("cuda") { .. }`** already parses and pushes onto
  `Environment::device_stack`; it currently falls back to CPU with a
  one-time warning because no CUDA dispatch exists.
- **Connect mode (SSE)** routes eval to any `mlpl-serve` peer; the
  `peer_dispatcher` abstraction dispatches a whole `device(...)`
  block server-side.

## Backend decision (the analog of MLX step 005's fork)

**Chosen: `candle`** (HuggingFace `candle-core` autograd via
`Tensor::backward()` + `candle-nn` optimizers, on `cudarc`). This
mirrors the MLX track's winning "approach A": use the framework's
built-in autodiff + optimizer, zero hand-written backward formulas.
Pure Rust, no multi-GB libtorch download. The load-bearing risk is
Blackwell sm_120 / CUDA 13.2 support in `cudarc`/`candle` -- the
step-1 spike de-risks exactly that before any wider work.

Rejected: `tch` (libtorch -- heavy + Blackwell/CUDA-13 build
freshness risk) and `cudarc`-only (= MLX "approach B", ~hand-written
kernels + autodiff, explicitly rejected on the MLX track).

## Crate plan (mirror the MLX crates 1:1)

| MLX crate | Role | CUDA crate to build |
|---|---|---|
| `mlpl-mlx-rt` | forward ops | `mlpl-cuda-rt` |
| `mlpl-mlx-forward` | embed / rms_norm / attention / cross-entropy | `mlpl-cuda-forward` |
| `mlpl-mlx-train` | autodiff + on-device Adam | `mlpl-cuda-train` |
| `mlpl-mlx-model` | `demo_forward` assembly | `mlpl-cuda-model` |
| `mlpl-mlx-serve` | server-side peer dispatcher | `mlpl-cuda-serve` |

All CUDA crates triple-gate `cfg(all(feature = "cuda", target_os =
"linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))`; absent any gate, dispatch is a
stub returning `None` and `device("cuda")` falls back to CPU with a
one-time warning (mirror `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs`).

## Steps

1. **cuda-backend-spike** -- add a gated spike crate; prove
   `candle` value/grad (`Tensor::backward`) + an Adam step reduce a
   tiny regression loss ON the RTX 5060 Ti. De-risk sm_120 / CUDA
   13.2 (pin candle/cudarc versions that support it; record the
   build incantation). Parity vs the analytic gradient. This is the
   go/no-go gate for candle.
2. **mlpl-cuda-rt** -- forward ops crate (matmul, elementwise,
   activations, softmax/reduce), gated; parity-tested vs CPU
   (`mlpl-array`).
3. **cuda-dispatch-wire** -- generalize `try_mlx_dispatch` /
   `dispatched_call` in `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` so `device("cuda")`
   routes through `mlpl-cuda-rt`; CPU fallback + one-time warning
   preserved; device dispatch tests extended for cuda.
4. **cuda-forward-and-model** -- `mlpl-cuda-forward` (embed,
   rms_norm, causal_attention, cross_entropy) + `mlpl-cuda-model`
   (`demo_forward`), each parity-tested vs the CPU primitives and
   the MLX reference.
5. **cuda-lora-demo** -- `mlpl-cuda-train` (candle autodiff +
   on-device Adam) wired into `eval_adam`'s CUDA branch (analog of
   `grad_optim_mlx.rs`); first CUDA demo `demos/lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl`
   + literate `examples/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.org`; flip the
   registry entry to runnable-on-connected-CUDA-peer. Parity: the
   `device("cuda")` LoRA loss curve matches the CPU path within fp32
   tol.
6. **cuda-connect-peer** -- `mlpl-cuda-serve` so
   `mlpl-serve --features cuda` on Linux is a connect-mode peer;
   add a `GET /api/devices` capability probe so the UI knows whether
   a connected server offers `mlx`, `cuda`, or neither, and gates
   demos by the live peer instead of a static guess. This is what
   makes "connect to a Mac and/or this Arch box" honest.

## Out of scope (this saga)

- Mirroring the other 3 MLX demos (tiny_lm, neural_thicket,
  mlx_remote) + their org docs -- a FOLLOW-UP saga once the vertical
  slice is green.
- SmolLM2 loader / LLaMA-style ops (saga `local-gpu-agentic`
  Phases 4-5, now CUDA candidates -- later).
- Agentic `:ask` Phase 2/3 -- parked on `main` as
  `local-gpu-agentic` step 011, platform-agnostic, pick up on
  either host.

## References

- `docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` -- the MLX track this mirrors;
  device tiers, "measurable learning" metric, demo-download policy.
- `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` -- the single dispatch site to generalize.
- `components/native-rt/crates/mlpl-mlx-{rt,forward,train}`,
  `components/mlx-model/`, `components/serve/.../mlpl-mlx-serve` --
  the crates to mirror.
- candle: <https://github.com/huggingface/candle>;
  cudarc Blackwell/CUDA-13 support is the step-1 spike's job to pin.

Build's still in early dependency compilation. Candle's CUDA kernel build takes several minutes; the harness will re-invoke me when it finishes, so I'll let it run rather than poll-burn. Here's where things stand.

## Done this session

**Pivot analysis** — The MLX (Apple) GPU track is complete; the plumbing is already CUDA-aware (`Device::Cuda` in the registry, `Value::DeviceTensor { device: "cuda" }`, `device("cuda")` parses and currently falls back to CPU). And critically: **this box (RTX 5060 Ti / Blackwell / CUDA 13.2) can actually build and test CUDA in-session**, unlike the Mac-only MLX track.

**Your `:ask` question** — answered above: Phases 0–1 shipped; **Phase 2 (server-side tool-using `/api/chat` loop with 6 context-provider tools + UI trace + result caps + host allow-list)** and **Phase 3 (RLM demo)** are parked. They're platform-agnostic, and your "local Ollama on the host first" scoping fits the existing server-side design with zero changes (host just defaults to `localhost:11434`). **Left fully live on `main` as `local-gpu-agentic` step 011** — `git checkout main` brings it right back.

**Saga set up** — On a new `cuda-foundation` branch (so `main` keeps the parked saga untouched — that's how I realized your "parked alongside" given agentrail is single-saga-per-repo). Plan in `docs/saga-cuda-foundation.md`, six steps:

1. **cuda-backend-spike** (GO/NO-GO — *in progress now*)
2. mlpl-cuda-rt (forward ops)
3. cuda-dispatch-wire (`device("cuda")` → cuda-rt in `device.rs`)
4. cuda-forward-and-model (`demo_forward`, exact CPU match)
5. cuda-lora-demo (first CUDA demo `.mlpl` + `.org` literate doc, parity vs CPU)
6. cuda-connect-peer (`mlpl-cuda-serve` + `GET /api/devices` so the UI gates by whether the connected Mac/Linux peer offers `mlx`/`cuda`)

**Step 1 started (candle, per your choice)** — scaffolded `components/cuda-rt/` as its own component workspace, with `mlpl-cuda-train` + a gated RED test (`spike_tests.rs`) that proves three things on the GPU: CUDA device init, autodiff gradient matches the closed-form least-squares gradient, and Adam collapses the loss. Building now with `CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=120`.

The build outcome is the real signal — if cudarc 0.17/0.19 supports sm_120 + CUDA 13.2, the spike likely goes green and I'll commit + `agentrail complete` step 1. If it rejects Blackwell, that's still a valid spike result and I'll pin a newer candle/cudarc (0.10.2 is available) or record the toolchain gap. I'll report when the build returns.

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

This first saga is the **foundation + one demo end-to-end**, proven
on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Why now, why here

This dev host is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell, sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA
13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, x86_64-linux-gnu, 1.6 TB free**. Unlike the
MLX track -- which this Linux box can never build or test -- a CUDA
track is fully buildable and TDD-testable in-session with real GPU
parity tests, not Apple-only glue.

## Foundation already in place (CUDA-aware plumbing)

- **`Device::Cuda`** exists in the web-demos registry
  (`mlpl-web-demos-types`), rendered visible-but-not-runnable on the
  public live demo.
- **`Value::DeviceTensor { device: String, .. }`** already names
  `"cuda"` as a future device (`mlpl-eval-types`).
- **`device("cuda") { .. }`** already parses and pushes onto
  `Environment::device_stack`; it currently falls back to CPU with a
  one-time warning because no CUDA dispatch exists.
- **Connect mode (SSE)** routes eval to any `mlpl-serve` peer; the
  `peer_dispatcher` abstraction dispatches a whole `device(...)`
  block server-side.

## Backend decision (the analog of MLX step 005's fork)

**Chosen: `candle`** (HuggingFace `candle-core` autograd via
`Tensor::backward()` + `candle-nn` optimizers, on `cudarc`). This
mirrors the MLX track's winning "approach A": use the framework's
built-in autodiff + optimizer, zero hand-written backward formulas.
Pure Rust, no multi-GB libtorch download. The load-bearing risk is
Blackwell sm_120 / CUDA 13.2 support in `cudarc`/`candle` -- the
step-1 spike de-risks exactly that before any wider work.

Rejected: `tch` (libtorch -- heavy + Blackwell/CUDA-13 build
freshness risk) and `cudarc`-only (= MLX "approach B", ~hand-written
kernels + autodiff, explicitly rejected on the MLX track).

## Crate plan (mirror the MLX crates 1:1)

| MLX crate | Role | CUDA crate to build |
|---|---|---|
| `mlpl-mlx-rt` | forward ops | `mlpl-cuda-rt` |
| `mlpl-mlx-forward` | embed / rms_norm / attention / cross-entropy | `mlpl-cuda-forward` |
| `mlpl-mlx-train` | autodiff + on-device Adam | `mlpl-cuda-train` |
| `mlpl-mlx-model` | `demo_forward` assembly | `mlpl-cuda-model` |
| `mlpl-mlx-serve` | server-side peer dispatcher | `mlpl-cuda-serve` |

All CUDA crates triple-gate `cfg(all(feature = "cuda", target_os =
"linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))`; absent any gate, dispatch is a
stub returning `None` and `device("cuda")` falls back to CPU with a
one-time warning (mirror `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs`).

## Steps

1. **cuda-backend-spike** -- add a gated spike crate; prove
   `candle` value/grad (`Tensor::backward`) + an Adam step reduce a
   tiny regression loss ON the RTX 5060 Ti. De-risk sm_120 / CUDA
   13.2 (pin candle/cudarc versions that support it; record the
   build incantation). Parity vs the analytic gradient. This is the
   go/no-go gate for candle.
2. **mlpl-cuda-rt** -- forward ops crate (matmul, elementwise,
   activations, softmax/reduce), gated; parity-tested vs CPU
   (`mlpl-array`).
3. **cuda-dispatch-wire** -- generalize `try_mlx_dispatch` /
   `dispatched_call` in `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` so `device("cuda")`
   routes through `mlpl-cuda-rt`; CPU fallback + one-time warning
   preserved; device dispatch tests extended for cuda.
4. **cuda-forward-and-model** -- `mlpl-cuda-forward` (embed,
   rms_norm, causal_attention, cross_entropy) + `mlpl-cuda-model`
   (`demo_forward`), each parity-tested vs the CPU primitives and
   the MLX reference.
5. **cuda-lora-demo** -- `mlpl-cuda-train` (candle autodiff +
   on-device Adam) wired into `eval_adam`'s CUDA branch (analog of
   `grad_optim_mlx.rs`); first CUDA demo `demos/lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl`
   + literate `examples/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.org`; flip the
   registry entry to runnable-on-connected-CUDA-peer. Parity: the
   `device("cuda")` LoRA loss curve matches the CPU path within fp32
   tol.
6. **cuda-connect-peer** -- `mlpl-cuda-serve` so
   `mlpl-serve --features cuda` on Linux is a connect-mode peer;
   add a `GET /api/devices` capability probe so the UI knows whether
   a connected server offers `mlx`, `cuda`, or neither, and gates
   demos by the live peer instead of a static guess. This is what
   makes "connect to a Mac and/or this Arch box" honest.

## Out of scope (this saga)

- Mirroring the other 3 MLX demos (tiny_lm, neural_thicket,
  mlx_remote) + their org docs -- a FOLLOW-UP saga once the vertical
  slice is green.
- SmolLM2 loader / LLaMA-style ops (saga `local-gpu-agentic`
  Phases 4-5, now CUDA candidates -- later).
- Agentic `:ask` Phase 2/3 -- parked on `main` as
  `local-gpu-agentic` step 011, platform-agnostic, pick up on
  either host.

## References

- `docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` -- the MLX track this mirrors;
  device tiers, "measurable learning" metric, demo-download policy.
- `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` -- the single dispatch site to generalize.
- `components/native-rt/crates/mlpl-mlx-{rt,forward,train}`,
  `components/mlx-model/`, `components/serve/.../mlpl-mlx-serve` --
  the crates to mirror.
- candle: <https://github.com/huggingface/candle>;
  cudarc Blackwell/CUDA-13 support is the step-1 spike's job to pin.

Confirmed the wiring: `pages/literate/` holds the org→html outputs plus an `index.html`, generated by `build-pages.sh`, and each demo carries a footer "literate-walkthrough" link. So mirroring the MLX literate doc in step 5 naturally produces `cuda-lora-finetune.html` + its index entry + the footer link.

## When you can review it

Honest answer in **steps**, not calendar dates (session cadence + how stiff the CPU-parity work turns out drive the clock, not me). The thing you described splits into two review points:

**Review point A — the CUDA org-mode page + index/footer link: end of step 5.**
That's 4 steps out (2 → 3 → 4 → 5). Steps 2–4 are unglamorous *engine* work with nothing user-visible (forward ops crate → `device("cuda")` dispatch wiring → forward primitives + `demo_forward` matching the CPU exactly). They're the prerequisite that makes the demo actually *compute* on this GPU. Step 5 is the first thing you can look at:
- `demos/lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl` running under `device("cuda")` on the RTX 5060 Ti,
- `examples/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.org` → `pages/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.html` (org-babel mlpl walkthrough, mirroring the MLX one),
- its entry in `pages/literate/index.html` and the demo's footer literate link,
- parity-asserted: the `device("cuda")` LoRA loss curve matches the CPU path.

**Review point B — the web UI connected to a server *here*, CUDA demos runnable: end of step 6 (the saga's last step).**
This is the piece you specifically asked about — `mlpl-serve --features cuda` running on this Arch box as a connect peer, plus `GET /api/devices` so the UI pointed at `?connect=<this-box>` *detects* CUDA and flips the CUDA demos from visible-but-not-runnable to runnable (exactly the MLX gating, but for this machine). Until step 6 lands, the step-5 org doc and demo source are reviewable but the demo shows as not-runnable in the UI, the same way MLX demos do on the public build.

So: **~4 steps to review the org-mode html + index/footer link, ~5 steps to the live connected-UI review.** Each step is roughly one commit/session like the spike you just saw.

Two things worth flagging:
- **Scope** — per your "foundation + 1 demo" choice, this saga delivers the *one* headline equivalent (CUDA LoRA fine-tune). "CUDA demos equivalent to the MLX ones" (all four — tiny_lm, neural_thicket, remote) is the **follow-up saga**; at the end of *this* one you review the LoRA equivalent fully connected, then we mirror the rest.
- The index-entry + footer-link requirement is captured (it falls out of "mirror the MLX literate doc" + `build-pages.sh`), and the connected-UI-runnable requirement is step 6's explicit deliverable — both are in `docs/saga-cuda-foundation.md`.

If you'd rather see the **connected UI sooner** (even against a single demo), I can reorder so the serve-peer + `/api/devices` + gating lands as soon as step 5's demo exists — but it can't meaningfully precede a runnable CUDA path, so steps 2–5 stay first either way.

That investigation settles it — and it actually flips your premise. Let me answer before continuing the build.

## The `_mlx` names are correct — nothing's mis-named

Both `_mlx` files genuinely use `device("mlx")` and exercise MLX (verified, and they're covered by real tests — `tiny_lm_mlx_demo_tests.rs`, `neural_thicket_mlx_demo_tests.rs`, plus the `mlx_vs_cpu` bench). The confusion was **two different files per demo**, not a mislabel:

| Demo | CPU/browser file (CPU tier) | MLX CLI variant (uses `device("mlx")`) |
|---|---|---|
| Tiny LM | `demos/tiny_lm.mlpl` | `demos/tiny_lm_mlx.mlpl` — forward (matmul/softmax/elementwise) runs on MLX; backward+Adam on CPU (hybrid) |
| Neural Thicket | `demos/neural_thicket.mlpl` | `demos/neural_thicket_mlx.mlpl` — the 16-variant inference sweep + ensemble runs on MLX; base training on CPU |

So when you said "Neural Thicket ran in the browser" / "tiny_lm used CPU" — that's true of the **unsuffixed** files (the web demos). The `_mlx` files are separate **CLI variants** that take that same source and wrap the compute in `device("mlx")` to exercise/validate the GPU path. The naming convention is consistent: `<demo>.mlpl` = CPU/web, `<demo>_mlx.mlpl` = MLX CLI variant. **No rename needed** — they really are MLX-related.

The one *clarity* nuance: `tiny_lm_mlx` and `neural_thicket_mlx` are **hybrid/partial** MLX (forward or inference on GPU, training on CPU), whereas only `lora_finetune_mlx` is full-GPU. - **MLX side:** add tic-tac-toe **CLI**; add Tiny LM **Web + org**; add Neural Thicket **Web + org**. (LoRA already done.)
- **CUDA side:** everything — 4 CLI + 4 Web + 4 org — built on the cuda-foundation engine.

**Proposed roadmap (3 sagas):**

1. **`cuda-foundation`** (in progress) — the engine (cuda-rt → dispatch → forward/model → train) + the **first** CUDA demo (LoRA) as the proven vertical slice: 1 CLI + 1 Web + 1 org.
2. **`mlx-demo-consolidation`** — fill the MLX gaps so all 4 have CLI+Web+org. Authoring (web entries, `.org` docs) is doable here on Linux; *running* the MLX path to validate needs a Mac, so this saga's parity tests are Apple-gated.

content.text:
`mlx_remote` is categorically different from the others — it's not an ML demo at all, it's an **architecture/plumbing demo**. Here's exactly what it shows and why it exists.

## What it demonstrates: remote device dispatch across two processes

The other demos run in one process. `mlx_remote` demonstrates the **orchestrator + peer split** — two separate `mlpl-serve`-family processes, possibly on two different machines, with `device("mlx")` work executed *on the remote one over HTTP*. From its own header:

```
# peer on the Apple Silicon host:
cargo run -- --bind 127.0.0.1:6465              # mlpl-mlx-serve
# orchestrator on the client host:
cargo run -p mlpl-serve -- --peer mlx=http://127.0.0.1:6465
```

So there's an **orchestrator** (`mlpl-serve`, where your REPL connects) and an **MLX peer** (`mlpl-mlx-serve`, on the Mac with the GPU). The orchestrator doesn't have a GPU; it forwards `device("mlx")` blocks to the peer.

## What each block proves (line by line)

**1. Remote evaluation + opaque device-tensor handles:**
```
remote_vec = device("mlx") { iota(5) }
remote_vec_cpu = to_device("cpu", remote_vec)
```
`iota(5)` runs *on the peer*. What comes back to the orchestrator is **not the data** — it's an opaque handle to a tensor that lives on the remote device (this is the `Value::DeviceTensor { peer, device, shape }` type we saw earlier; touching it CPU-side faults). To actually see numbers you must **explicitly fetch them** with `to_device("cpu", …)`. That explicit-fetch discipline is the whole point: data doesn't silently cross the network; the program says when bytes move.

**2. A whole training loop executing remotely, only the result fetched back:**
```
losses = device("mlx") {
  X = reshape(iota(16), [2, 8]); Y = X
  model = chain(linear(8,16,0), tanh_layer(), linear(16,8,1))
  to_device("mlx", X); to_device("mlx", Y)
  train 8 { pred = apply(model, X); diff = pred - Y; loss = mean(diff*diff); adam(...); loss }
}
losses_cpu = to_device("cpu", losses)
```
The model, the forward, the MSE, and 8 Adam steps **all run on the remote GPU**; only the loss curve is pulled back. Note the model/task is deliberately trivial — `X = Y` (fitting identity-ish on `iota` data). **There's no measurable learning, no held-out metric, no interesting model.** The ML content is a placeholder. What's being exercised is: can a full `train { … }` block execute end-to-end on a remote peer and return just its scalar outputs?

## So "a demo of what?"

Of the **distributed/remote-GPU transport layer**, specifically four mechanisms:
1. orchestrator → peer dispatch of `device(...)` blocks over HTTP,
2. **opaque device-tensor handles** that stay resident on the peer,
3. **explicit `to_device` data movement** across the process/network boundary (no silent transfers),
4. a complete training loop surviving that round-trip.

It's an **infrastructure smoke test**, not a machine-learning showcase. That's why it's the odd one out: the saga's success metric for "real demos" is *measurable learning on held-out data*, and `mlx_remote` has none — by design.

## Why this matters for your decision

This is directly germane to your "**UI connects to a server on a Mac and/or Arch Linux**" goal. `mlx_remote` is essentially the **prototype of that connect-to-a-remote-GPU capability** — it's the spiritual ancestor of cuda-foundation **step 6** (`mlpl-cuda-serve` peer + `/api/devices`). So I'd argue it shouldn't be one of the "4 ML demos" (it doesn't tell an ML story), but it also shouldn't be discarded — it's better treated as a **capability/architecture demo** that documents the peer transport, living alongside the connect-peer work rather than in the 4×{CLI,Web,org} ML matrix.

That's the reasoning behind my recommendation to make the canonical 4 = **LoRA, Tiny LM, Neural Thicket, tic-tac-toe** (the four distinct ML stories) and keep `mlx_remote` as a separate transport demo. But if you'd rather the matrix *be* the four CLI files as they exist today (which includes `mlx_remote` and excludes tic-tac-toe), that's the real fork — which is why I asked.

Want me to re-pose the canonical-set question with this framing, or do you already know which way you want to go?

# GPU demos + multi-backend connect -- program roadmap

The grand arc: a complete, symmetric set of GPU demos across **MLX
(Apple)** and **CUDA (NVIDIA/Linux)**, each demo present as a CLI
script, a connect-mode web demo, and an org-mode literate doc; plus
a remote/transport demo per backend; building toward a UI that can
connect to **two backends at once** (MLX + CUDA) for side-by-side
comparison, and eventually to **two CUDA peers with different GPUs**
for N-way hardware comparison.

This doc is the program-level plan. Individual sagas
(`docs/saga-*.md`) implement slices of it.

## Demo taxonomy

### Group A -- ML demos (the matrix)

Four *distinct ML stories*, each with measurable learning on
held-out data (the project's demo success metric):

1. **LoRA fine-tune** -- full-GPU LoRA adapter fine-tune of a tiny LM.
2. **Tiny LM** -- pretrain a tiny language model (perplexity drop).
3. **Neural Thicket** -- ensemble variant sweep + inference.
4. **tic-tac-toe fine-tune** -- self-play RL fine-tune.

Target: each demo as **CLI + Web + org**, for **MLX + CUDA** =
`4 demos x 3 surfaces x 2 backends = 24 artifacts`.

### Group B -- remote / transport demos

Not ML demos -- they exercise the orchestrator/peer transport:
remote `device(...)` dispatch, opaque device-tensor handles, and
explicit `to_device` data movement across the process/network
boundary.

- **mlx_remote** (exists, CLI only) and **cuda_remote** (new twin).

Target: each as CLI + Web + org, grouped under a "Remote / Connect"
section in the UI (distinct from the ML demo groups) =
`2 demos x 3 surfaces = 6 artifacts`.

### Group C -- comparison demos (emergent, later sagas)

Side-by-side runs of one workload across multiple connected peers
(MLX vs CUDA; CUDA-A vs CUDA-B). These are views/demos that build
on the multi-backend connect work below.

## Current state (2026-06-02)

| Demo | CLI | Web | org | MLX status |
|------|-----|-----|-----|------------|
| LoRA fine-tune | yes | yes | yes | COMPLETE |
| tic-tac-toe | no  | yes | yes | needs CLI |
| Tiny LM | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |
| Neural Thicket | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |
| mlx_remote | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |

CUDA side: nothing yet (cuda-foundation builds the engine + the
first CUDA demo). Only **LoRA fine-tune** is currently complete on
any backend.

## Connect architecture arc

1. **Single connect** -- UI connects to ONE peer (Mac MLX or Arch
   CUDA); a `GET /api/devices` probe reports what that server
   offers (`cpu`/`mlx`/`cuda`) and the UI gates demos by it. (This
   is `cuda-foundation` step 6.)
2. **Dual backend** -- UI connects to an MLX peer AND a CUDA peer
   at once; run the same demo on both; render side-by-side
   (loss curves, wall-clock, output diff within tol). The
   orchestrator already holds multiple named peers
   (`--peer mlx=... --peer cuda=...`, `PeerRegistry`); the work is
   comparison orchestration + UI + aggregated `/api/devices`.
3. **N-way same-device** -- two+ CUDA peers with DIFFERENT GPUs
   (e.g. RTX 5060 Ti vs another card). Generalize the registry to
   multiple peers per device-type (keys like `cuda_a`, `cuda_b`)
   and add GPU identity (name, memory, compute-cap) to
   `/api/devices` so the UI labels each comparison column.

## Cross-cutting: define-once consolidation

Today a demo's source can live in three places (the `.mlpl` CLI
file, an inline string in the web registry, and the `.org` doc),
which is why coverage drifted. The consolidation principle: **one
canonical `.mlpl` per demo is the source of truth**; the
web-registry entry and the `.org` literate doc are derived/extracted
from it by tooling. Introduced in the MLX consolidation saga so the
CUDA saga inherits it.

Also relevant: **3D viz passthrough** (see
`docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` Phase 1c) -- comparison views need
viz data to flow back from peers, not just a display string.

## Saga roadmap

1. **cuda-foundation** (ACTIVE) -- CUDA engine (`mlpl-cuda-rt` ->
   dispatch -> forward/model -> train) + the first CUDA demo (LoRA:
   CLI + Web + org) + single-connect peer (`mlpl-cuda-serve` +
   `/api/devices`). Proves the whole vertical slice on this box.
2. **mlx-demo-consolidation** -- the define-once tooling, then fill
   the MLX gaps: tic-tac-toe CLI; Tiny LM Web + org; Neural Thicket
   Web + org; mlx_remote Web + org. Result: MLX = 4 ML x (CLI+Web+
   org) + mlx_remote x (CLI+Web+org). MLX runtime parity tests are
   Apple-gated (authoring is doable on Linux; execution needs a Mac).
3. **cuda-demo-parity** -- CUDA equivalents for the remaining 3 ML
   demos (tic-tac-toe, Tiny LM, Neural Thicket) + cuda_remote, using
   the define-once tooling. Result: CUDA = 4 ML x (CLI+Web+org) +
   cuda_remote. Fully testable on this box.
4. **dual-backend-connect** -- run one workload across MLX + CUDA
   peers simultaneously; side-by-side comparison view; aggregated
   `/api/devices`; a "Compare backends" demo (Group C).
5. **nway-gpu-compare** -- two+ CUDA peers with different GPUs;
   multi-peer-per-device registry + GPU-identity metadata; N-column
   comparison UI; a "two CUDA GPUs" benchmark demo.

After saga 3 the full `24 + 6` artifact matrix exists; sagas 4-5
add the comparison superpowers on top.

## End-state scorecard

- MLX: 4 ML demos x (CLI + Web + org) + mlx_remote x (CLI+Web+org)
- CUDA: 4 ML demos x (CLI + Web + org) + cuda_remote x (CLI+Web+org)
- UI: connect to 1 peer (gate by device); 2 peers (MLX vs CUDA
  compare); N CUDA peers (different GPUs compare).

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

This first saga is the **foundation + one demo end-to-end**, proven
on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Why now, why here

This dev host is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell, sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA
13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, x86_64-linux-gnu, 1.6 TB free**. Unlike the
MLX track -- which this Linux box can never build or test -- a CUDA
track is fully buildable and TDD-testable in-session with real GPU
parity tests, not Apple-only glue.

## Foundation already in place (CUDA-aware plumbing)

- **`Device::Cuda`** exists in the web-demos registry
  (`mlpl-web-demos-types`), rendered visible-but-not-runnable on the
  public live demo.
- **`Value::DeviceTensor { device: String, .. }`** already names
  `"cuda"` as a future device (`mlpl-eval-types`).
- **`device("cuda") { .. }`** already parses and pushes onto
  `Environment::device_stack`; it currently falls back to CPU with a

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Serving + LAN access (requirement)

The dev workflow needs a remote LAN client (e.g. a laptop) to reach
the connect server + web UI running on this Arch box. Reality today:

- `mlpl-serve --bind 0.0.0.0:6464` already binds on all interfaces;
  non-loopback binds REQUIRE `--auth required` (auth-disabled is
  loopback-only, a deliberate RCE guard -- the server evaluates
  arbitrary pasted MLPL).
- The same `mlpl-serve` serves the web playground via
  `--static-dir <web-dist>` at `<scheme>://<bind>/sw-mlpl/`.
- So one process is both the static UI host and the connect target.

The CUDA connect-peer step (saga 1, step 7) must therefore verify
the LAN path end to end, not just loopback: bind `0.0.0.0`, serve
the UI, connect a remote browser via `?connect=`, and confirm the
SSE eval stream + `/api/devices` work cross-host. The known gotcha
is TLS/CORS over the LAN: the self-signed cert is loopback-only, so
a LAN client needs either plain HTTP (browser mixed-content / SSE
caveats) or a cert valid for the box's LAN name/IP. Resolve this in
step 7.

# GPU demos + multi-backend connect -- program roadmap

The grand arc: a complete, symmetric set of GPU demos across **MLX
(Apple)** and **CUDA (NVIDIA/Linux)**, each demo present as a CLI
script, a connect-mode web demo, and an org-mode literate doc; plus
a remote/transport demo per backend; building toward a UI that can
connect to **two backends at once** (MLX + CUDA) for side-by-side
comparison, and eventually to **two CUDA peers with different GPUs**
for N-way hardware comparison.

This doc is the program-level plan. Individual sagas
(`docs/saga-*.md`) implement slices of it.

## Demo taxonomy

### Group A -- ML demos (the matrix)

Four *distinct ML stories*, each with measurable learning on
held-out data (the project's demo success metric):

1. **LoRA fine-tune** -- full-GPU LoRA adapter fine-tune of a tiny LM.
2. **Tiny LM** -- pretrain a tiny language model (perplexity drop).
3. **Neural Thicket** -- ensemble variant sweep + inference.
4. **tic-tac-toe fine-tune** -- self-play RL fine-tune.

Target: each demo as **CLI + Web + org**, for **MLX + CUDA** =
`4 demos x 3 surfaces x 2 backends = 24 artifacts`.

### Group B -- remote / transport demos

Not ML demos -- they exercise the orchestrator/peer transport:
remote `device(...)` dispatch, opaque device-tensor handles, and
explicit `to_device` data movement across the process/network
boundary.

- **mlx_remote** (exists, CLI only) and **cuda_remote** (new twin).

Target: each as CLI + Web + org, grouped under a "Remote / Connect"
section in the UI (distinct from the ML demo groups) =
`2 demos x 3 surfaces = 6 artifacts`.

### Group C -- comparison demos (emergent, later sagas)

Side-by-side runs of one workload across multiple connected peers
(MLX vs CUDA; CUDA-A vs CUDA-B). These are views/demos that build
on the multi-backend connect work below.

## Current state (2026-06-02)

| Demo | CLI | Web | org | MLX status |
|------|-----|-----|-----|------------|
| LoRA fine-tune | yes | yes | yes | COMPLETE |
| tic-tac-toe | no  | yes | yes | needs CLI |
| Tiny LM | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |
| Neural Thicket | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |
| mlx_remote | yes | no | no | needs Web + org |

CUDA side: nothing yet (cuda-foundation builds the engine + the
first CUDA demo). Only **LoRA fine-tune** is currently complete on
any backend.

## Connect architecture arc

1. **Single connect** -- UI connects to ONE peer (Mac MLX or Arch
   CUDA); a `GET /api/devices` probe reports what that server
   offers (`cpu`/`mlx`/`cuda`) and the UI gates demos by it. (This
   is `cuda-foundation` step 6.)
2. **Dual backend** -- UI connects to an MLX peer AND a CUDA peer
   at once; run the same demo on both; render side-by-side
   (loss curves, wall-clock, output diff within tol). The
   orchestrator already holds multiple named peers
   (`--peer mlx=... --peer cuda=...`, `PeerRegistry`); the work is
   comparison orchestration + UI + aggregated `/api/devices`.
3. **N-way same-device** -- two+ CUDA peers with DIFFERENT GPUs
   (e.g. RTX 5060 Ti vs another card). Generalize the registry to
   multiple peers per device-type (keys like `cuda_a`, `cuda_b`)
   and add GPU identity (name, memory, compute-cap) to
   `/api/devices` so the UI labels each comparison column.

## Cross-cutting: define-once consolidation

Today a demo's source can live in three places (the `.mlpl` CLI
file, an inline string in the web registry, and the `.org` doc),
which is why coverage drifted. The consolidation principle: **one
canonical `.mlpl` per demo is the source of truth**; the
web-registry entry and the `.org` literate doc are derived/extracted
from it by tooling. Introduced in the MLX consolidation saga so the
CUDA saga inherits it.

Also relevant: **3D viz passthrough** (see
`docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` Phase 1c) -- comparison views need
viz data to flow back from peers, not just a display string.

## Saga roadmap

1. **cuda-foundation** (ACTIVE) -- CUDA engine (`mlpl-cuda-rt` ->
   dispatch -> forward/model -> train) + the first CUDA demo (LoRA:
   CLI + Web + org) + single-connect peer (`mlpl-cuda-serve` +
   `/api/devices`). Proves the whole vertical slice on this box.
2. **mlx-demo-consolidation** -- the define-once tooling, then fill
   the MLX gaps: tic-tac-toe CLI; Tiny LM Web + org; Neural Thicket
   Web + org; mlx_remote Web + org. Result: MLX = 4 ML x (CLI+Web+
   org) + mlx_remote x (CLI+Web+org). MLX runtime parity tests are
   Apple-gated (authoring is doable on Linux; execution needs a Mac).
3. **cuda-demo-parity** -- CUDA equivalents for the remaining 3 ML
   demos (tic-tac-toe, Tiny LM, Neural Thicket) + cuda_remote, using
   the define-once tooling. Result: CUDA = 4 ML x (CLI+Web+org) +
   cuda_remote. Fully testable on this box.
4. **dual-backend-connect** -- run one workload across MLX + CUDA
   peers simultaneously; side-by-side comparison view; aggregated
   `/api/devices`; a "Compare backends" demo (Group C).
5. **nway-gpu-compare** -- two+ CUDA peers with different GPUs;
   multi-peer-per-device registry + GPU-identity metadata; N-column
   comparison UI; a "two CUDA GPUs" benchmark demo.

After saga 3 the full `24 + 6` artifact matrix exists; sagas 4-5
add the comparison superpowers on top.

## End-state scorecard

- MLX: 4 ML demos x (CLI + Web + org) + mlx_remote x (CLI+Web+org)
- CUDA: 4 ML demos x (CLI + Web + org) + cuda_remote x (CLI+Web+org)
- UI: connect to 1 peer (gate by device); 2 peers (MLX vs CUDA
  compare); N CUDA peers (different GPUs compare).

Step 2 is committed and pushed, and your LAN requirement is captured in the roadmap. Here's the answer to your question.

## Today, right now (no CUDA demos yet)

You can already serve the web UI on your LAN and connect to it — this works on the current `main`/branch without any CUDA work:

```bash
mlpl-serve --bind 0.0.0.0:6464 --auth required --static-dir <web-dist>
```

- **`0.0.0.0` LAN bind is already supported.** The one guard: non-loopback binds **require `--auth required`** (auth-disabled is loopback-only, because the server evaluates arbitrary pasted MLPL — that'd be RCE on your LAN). Default auth is already `required`, so you're fine.
- The **same process serves the web UI** (`--static-dir`) at `http(s)://<box-ip>:6464/sw-mlpl/` **and** is the connect target. A remote browser loads it and uses `?connect=` to route eval here.
- **The catch for LAN:** TLS is self-signed loopback-only, so a LAN client needs either plain HTTP (browser SSE/mixed-content caveats) or a cert valid for the box's LAN IP/name. That's the real thing to nail down — I've written it into step 7.

At this point you'd see the existing CPU/connect demos; **CUDA demos exist but render not-runnable** (no CUDA dispatch yet).

## When CUDA demos become real — staged

Steps remaining (numbers shifted after I inserted `cuda-nn`): **3** cuda-nn → **4** cuda-dispatch-wire → **5** cuda-forward-and-model → **6** cuda-lora-demo → **7** cuda-connect-peer.

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

This first saga is the **foundation + one demo end-to-end**, proven
on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Why now, why here

This dev host is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell, sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA
13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, x86_64-linux-gnu, 1.6 TB free**. Unlike the
MLX track -- which this Linux box can never build or test -- a CUDA
track is fully buildable and TDD-testable in-session with real GPU
parity tests, not Apple-only glue.

## Foundation already in place (CUDA-aware plumbing)

- **`Device::Cuda`** exists in the web-demos registry
  (`mlpl-web-demos-types`), rendered visible-but-not-runnable on the
  public live demo.
- **`Value::DeviceTensor { device: String, .. }`** already names
  `"cuda"` as a future device (`mlpl-eval-types`).
- **`device("cuda") { .. }`** already parses and pushes onto
  `Environment::device_stack`; it currently falls back to CPU with a
  one-time warning because no CUDA dispatch exists.
- **Connect mode (SSE)** routes eval to any `mlpl-serve` peer; the
  `peer_dispatcher` abstraction dispatches a whole `device(...)`
  block server-side.

## Backend decision (the analog of MLX step 005's fork)

**Chosen: `candle`** (HuggingFace `candle-core` autograd via
`Tensor::backward()` + `candle-nn` optimizers, on `cudarc`). This
mirrors the MLX track's winning "approach A": use the framework's
built-in autodiff + optimizer, zero hand-written backward formulas.
Pure Rust, no multi-GB libtorch download. The load-bearing risk is
Blackwell sm_120 / CUDA 13.2 support in `cudarc`/`candle` -- the
step-1 spike de-risks exactly that before any wider work.

Rejected: `tch` (libtorch -- heavy + Blackwell/CUDA-13 build
freshness risk) and `cudarc`-only (= MLX "approach B", ~hand-written
kernels + autodiff, explicitly rejected on the MLX track).

## Crate plan (mirror the MLX crates 1:1)

| MLX crate | Role | CUDA crate to build |
|---|---|---|
| `mlpl-mlx-rt` | forward ops | `mlpl-cuda-rt` (matmul/shape/convert) + `mlpl-cuda-elementwise` (arith) + `mlpl-cuda-nn` (activations/reductions) |
| `mlpl-mlx-forward` | embed / rms_norm / attention / cross-entropy | `mlpl-cuda-forward` |
| `mlpl-mlx-train` | autodiff + on-device Adam | `mlpl-cuda-train` |
| `mlpl-mlx-model` | `demo_forward` assembly | `mlpl-cuda-model` |
| `mlpl-mlx-serve` | server-side peer dispatcher | `mlpl-cuda-serve` |

All CUDA crates triple-gate `cfg(all(feature = "cuda", target_os =
"linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))`; absent any gate, dispatch is a
stub returning `None` and `device("cuda")` falls back to CPU with a
one-time warning (mirror `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs`).

## Steps

1. **cuda-backend-spike** -- DONE (GO). Gated crate
   `components/cuda-rt/crates/mlpl-cuda-train` proves candle's CUDA
   backend on the RTX 5060 Ti: 3 GPU tests pass (device init,
   autodiff gradient == closed-form least-squares gradient, Adam
   collapses the loss on-device). Pinned candle-core/nn 0.9.2 +
   cudarc 0.19.7 build for `sm_120` / CUDA 13.2; build incantation
   in the crate README (`CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=120`, `/opt/cuda` env).
   candle (approach A) confirmed viable -- the rest of the saga
   proceeds on it.
2. **mlpl-cuda-rt** -- DONE. The core tensor ops split into two
   warning-free sibling crates (the eager surface is too large for
   one crate under the <=4 fn/module + <=4 module/crate budgets):
   `mlpl-cuda-rt` (convert/device plumbing, `matmul`, `reshape`,
   `transpose`) and `mlpl-cuda-elementwise` (`add`/`sub`/`mul`/`div`
   with scalar broadcast, `neg`). Both gated; 6 GPU parity tests
   pass vs the CPU path within fp32 tol. The nn surface
   (activations, softmax/reduce, `cross_entropy`) is split out to
   step 2b (`mlpl-cuda-nn`): candle lacks a `prod` reduction and
   `cross_entropy` parity is fiddly, and those ops overlap the
   step-4 candle forward.
2b. **mlpl-cuda-nn** -- activations (`exp`/`log`/`relu`/`sigmoid`/
   `tanh`), reductions (`mean`/`reduce_mul`/`argmax`), and
   `softmax`/`log_softmax`/`cross_entropy` over candle, parity-tested
   vs CPU. `reduce_mul` may delegate to CPU (candle has no `prod`).
3. **cuda-dispatch-wire** -- generalize `try_mlx_dispatch` /
   `dispatched_call` in `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` so `device("cuda")`
   routes through `mlpl-cuda-rt`; CPU fallback + one-time warning
   preserved; device dispatch tests extended for cuda.
4. **cuda-forward-and-model** -- `mlpl-cuda-forward` (embed,
   rms_norm, causal_attention, cross_entropy) + `mlpl-cuda-model`
   (`demo_forward`), each parity-tested vs the CPU primitives and
   the MLX reference.
5. **cuda-lora-demo** -- `mlpl-cuda-train` (candle autodiff +
   on-device Adam) wired into `eval_adam`'s CUDA branch (analog of
   `grad_optim_mlx.rs`); first CUDA demo `demos/lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl`
   + literate `examples/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.org`; flip the
   registry entry to runnable-on-connected-CUDA-peer. Parity: the
   `device("cuda")` LoRA loss curve matches the CPU path within fp32
   tol.
6. **cuda-connect-peer** -- `mlpl-cuda-serve` so
   `mlpl-serve --features cuda` on Linux is a connect-mode peer;
   add a `GET /api/devices` capability probe so the UI knows whether
   a connected server offers `mlx`, `cuda`, or neither, and gates
   demos by the live peer instead of a static guess. This is what
   makes "connect to a Mac and/or this Arch box" honest.

## Out of scope (this saga)

- Mirroring the other 3 MLX demos (tiny_lm, neural_thicket,
  mlx_remote) + their org docs -- a FOLLOW-UP saga once the vertical
  slice is green.
- SmolLM2 loader / LLaMA-style ops (saga `local-gpu-agentic`
  Phases 4-5, now CUDA candidates -- later).
- Agentic `:ask` Phase 2/3 -- parked on `main` as
  `local-gpu-agentic` step 011, platform-agnostic, pick up on
  either host.

## References

- `docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` -- the MLX track this mirrors;
  device tiers, "measurable learning" metric, demo-download policy.
- `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` -- the single dispatch site to generalize.
- `components/native-rt/crates/mlpl-mlx-{rt,forward,train}`,
  `components/mlx-model/`, `components/serve/.../mlpl-mlx-serve` --
  the crates to mirror.
- candle: <https://github.com/huggingface/candle>;
  cudarc Blackwell/CUDA-13 support is the step-1 spike's job to pin.

99	/// Dispatch a named op through `mlpl-mlx-rt` when the running build
100	/// supports it. Returns `None` to mean "this op is not in the
101	/// MLX surface, run it on CPU"; `Some(Ok(arr))` for a successful
102	/// MLX result; `Some(Err(e))` for an MLX-side validation error
103	/// (caller should surface it the same way the CPU path would).
104	#[cfg(all(feature = "mlx", target_os = "macos", target_arch = "aarch64"))]
105	pub(crate) fn try_mlx_dispatch(
106	    name: &str,
107	    args: &[DenseArray],
108	) -> Option<Result<DenseArray, ArrayError>> {
109	    use mlpl_mlx_rt as mx;
110	    Some(match (name, args.len()) {
111	        ("matmul", 2) => mx::matmul(&args[0], &args[1]),
112	        ("add", 2) => mx::add(&args[0], &args[1]),
113	        ("sub", 2) => mx::sub(&args[0], &args[1]),
114	        ("mul", 2) => mx::mul(&args[0], &args[1]),
115	        ("div", 2) => mx::div(&args[0], &args[1]),
116	        ("neg", 1) => Ok(mx::neg(&args[0])),
117	        ("exp", 1) => Ok(mx::exp(&args[0])),
118	        ("log", 1) => Ok(mx::log(&args[0])),

1	//! `device("target") { body }` evaluator + MLX dispatch helper
2	//! (Saga 14 step 004).
3	//!
4	//! Two responsibilities live here:
5	//!
6	//! 1. `eval_device` runs the body of a `device("...")` block with
7	//!    the named target pushed onto `Environment::device_stack`. On
8	//!    exit it pops the entry, restoring whatever target was active
9	//!    in the surrounding scope. Nesting works in either direction
10	//!    (`experiment { device { ... } }` and the swap), and an inner
11	//!    `device("cpu")` overrides an outer `device("mlx")`.
12	//!
13	//! 2. `try_mlx_dispatch` is the single place where `mlpl-eval`
14	//!    decides whether an op should route through the `mlpl-mlx-rt`
15	//!    runtime. It is called from `eval_binop` and `eval_fncall`
16	//!    only when `Environment::device()` returns `"mlx"`. The
17	//!    helper returns `Some(result)` if the named op exists in
18	//!    `mlpl-mlx-rt`, otherwise `None` so the caller can fall back to
19	//!    the CPU path.
20	//!
21	//! Triple-gate: the `mlx` Cargo feature on `mlpl-eval` pulls in
22	//! `mlpl-mlx-rt` (which itself triple-gates on
23	//! `target_os = "macos"`, `target_arch = "aarch64"`, and its own
24	//! `mlx` feature). When any of those is missing the dispatch
25	//! helper is a stub returning `None`, the `device("mlx") { }`
26	//! block falls back to CPU, and `eval_device` emits a one-time
27	//! warning so the user knows their code ran on the wrong device.
28	
29	use mlpl_array::{ArrayError, DenseArray};
30	use mlpl_array_ops_element::prelude::*;
31	use mlpl_parser::Expr;
32	use mlpl_trace::Trace;
33	
34	use crate::env::Environment;
35	use mlpl_eval_types::EvalError;
36	use mlpl_eval_types::Value;
37	
38	/// Evaluate a `device("target") { body }` block. Returns the
39	/// value of the body's last statement -- mirrors `experiment`'s
40	/// shape so a `device(...)` block is a value-yielding expression
41	/// like every other scoped form.
42	pub(crate) fn eval_device(
43	    target: &str,
44	    body: &[Expr],
45	    env: &mut Environment,
46	    trace: &mut Option<&mut Trace>,
47	) -> Result<Value, EvalError> {
48	    if let Some(dispatcher) = env.peer_dispatcher() {
49	        let source = block_source(body);
50	        let bindings = collect_array_bindings(env, &source);
51	        if let Some(result) = dispatcher.dispatch_block(target, &source, bindings) {
52	            return result;
53	        }
54	    }
55	    if !device_available(target) && env.take_device_fallback_warning() {
56	        eprintln!(
57	            "warning: device(\"{target}\") block requested but the \
58	             {target} feature is not compiled in; falling back to CPU."
59	        );
60	    }
61	    env.push_device(target.to_string());
62	    let mut last = Value::Array(DenseArray::from_scalar(0.0));
63	    for stmt in body {
64	        last = crate::eval::eval_expr(stmt, env, trace)?;
65	    }
66	    env.pop_device();
67	    Ok(last)
68	}
69	
70	fn block_source(body: &[Expr]) -> String {
71	    body.iter()
72	        .map(std::string::ToString::to_string)
73	        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
74	        .join("\n")
75	}
76	
77	fn collect_array_bindings(
78	    env: &Environment,
79	    source: &str,
80	) -> std::collections::HashMap<String, DenseArray> {
81	    env.vars_iter()
82	        .filter(|(name, _)| source.contains(name.as_str()))
83	        .map(|(name, arr)| (name.clone(), arr.clone()))
84	        .collect()
85	}
86	
87	/// Whether the running build can dispatch through MLX (Apple) or
88	/// CUDA (Linux). Each combines its Cargo feature gate with the
89	/// target gate so the rest of the module branches on a single bool.
90	const fn mlx_available() -> bool {
91	    cfg!(all(
92	        feature = "mlx",
93	        target_os = "macos",
94	        target_arch = "aarch64"
95	    ))
96	}
97	const fn cuda_available() -> bool {
98	    cfg!(all(
99	        feature = "cuda",
100	        target_os = "linux",
101	        target_arch = "x86_64"
102	    ))
103	}
104	
105	/// Whether `target`'s backend can dispatch in this build (`cpu` is
106	/// always available). Drives the one-time CPU-fallback warning.
107	fn device_available(target: &str) -> bool {
108	    match target {
109	        "mlx" => mlx_available(),
110	        "cuda" => cuda_available(),
111	        _ => true,
112	    }
113	}
114	
115	/// Map a named op + args onto `$backend`'s primitive surface and
116	/// return `Some(result)` for a known op, `None` to fall back to CPU.
117	/// MLX and CUDA expose an identical surface (same signatures, same
118	/// `Result`/infallible split), so both dispatchers are generated
119	/// from this one definition (loose-coupling: define once).
120	#[allow(unused_macros)] // unused on CPU-only builds (neither GPU backend gated in).
121	macro_rules! op_dispatch {
122	    ($backend:path, $name:expr, $args:expr) => {{
123	        use $backend as b;
124	        let args = $args;
125	        Some(match ($name, args.len()) {
126	            ("matmul", 2) => b::matmul(&args[0], &args[1]),
127	            ("add", 2) => b::add(&args[0], &args[1]),
128	            ("sub", 2) => b::sub(&args[0], &args[1]),
129	            ("mul", 2) => b::mul(&args[0], &args[1]),
130	            ("div", 2) => b::div(&args[0], &args[1]),
131	            ("neg", 1) => Ok(b::neg(&args[0])),
132	            ("exp", 1) => Ok(b::exp(&args[0])),
133	            ("log", 1) => Ok(b::log(&args[0])),
134	            ("relu", 1) => Ok(b::relu(&args[0])),
135	            ("sigmoid", 1) => Ok(b::sigmoid(&args[0])),
136	            ("tanh" | "tanh_fn", 1) => Ok(b::tanh(&args[0])),
137	            ("transpose", 1) => Ok(b::transpose(&args[0])),
138	            ("reshape", 2) => {
139	                let dims: Vec<usize> = args[1].data().iter().map(|&d| d as usize).collect();
140	                b::reshape(&args[0], &dims)
141	            }
142	            ("softmax", 2) => b::softmax(&args[0], args[1].data()[0] as usize),
143	            ("log_softmax", 2) => b::log_softmax(&args[0], args[1].data()[0] as usize),
144	            ("cross_entropy", 2) => b::cross_entropy(&args[0], &args[1]),
145	            ("reduce_mul", 1) => b::reduce_mul(&args[0], None),
146	            ("reduce_mul", 2) => b::reduce_mul(&args[0], Some(args[1].data()[0] as usize)),
147	            ("mean", 1) => b::mean(&args[0], None),
148	            ("mean", 2) => b::mean(&args[0], Some(args[1].data()[0] as usize)),
149	            ("argmax", 1) => b::argmax(&args[0], None),
150	            ("argmax", 2) => b::argmax(&args[0], Some(args[1].data()[0] as usize)),
151	            _ => return None,
152	        })
153	    }};
154	}
155	
156	/// Dispatch a named op through `mlpl-mlx-rt` (Apple build) or CPU.
157	/// `Some(_)` = handled by MLX; `None` = run on CPU.
158	#[cfg(all(feature = "mlx", target_os = "macos", target_arch = "aarch64"))]
159	#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation, clippy::cast_sign_loss)] // dims/axis from validated f64 array values.
160	pub(crate) fn try_mlx_dispatch(
161	    name: &str,
162	    args: &[DenseArray],
163	) -> Option<Result<DenseArray, ArrayError>> {
164	    op_dispatch!(mlpl_mlx_rt, name, args)
165	}
166	
167	/// Stub for builds without MLX support: always CPU fallback.
168	#[cfg(not(all(feature = "mlx", target_os = "macos", target_arch = "aarch64")))]
169	pub(crate) fn try_mlx_dispatch(
170	    _name: &str,
171	    _args: &[DenseArray],
172	) -> Option<Result<DenseArray, ArrayError>> {
173	    None
174	}
175	
176	/// The CUDA op surface unified under one path so `op_dispatch!` can
177	/// drive it the same way as `mlpl_mlx_rt` (the ops live across three
178	/// sibling crates).
179	#[cfg(all(feature = "cuda", target_os = "linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
180	mod cuda_ops {
181	    pub use mlpl_cuda_elementwise::{add, div, exp, log, mul, neg, relu, sigmoid, sub, tanh};
182	    pub use mlpl_cuda_nn::{argmax, cross_entropy, log_softmax, mean, reduce_mul, softmax};
183	    pub use mlpl_cuda_rt::{matmul, reshape, transpose};
184	}
185

1	//! `device("target") { body }` evaluator + MLX dispatch helper
2	//! (Saga 14 step 004).
3	//!
4	//! Two responsibilities live here:
5	//!
6	//! 1. `eval_device` runs the body of a `device("...")` block with
7	//!    the named target pushed onto `Environment::device_stack`. On
8	//!    exit it pops the entry, restoring whatever target was active
9	//!    in the surrounding scope. Nesting works in either direction
10	//!    (`experiment { device { ... } }` and the swap), and an inner
11	//!    `device("cpu")` overrides an outer `device("mlx")`.
12	//!
13	//! 2. `try_mlx_dispatch` is the single place where `mlpl-eval`
14	//!    decides whether an op should route through the `mlpl-mlx-rt`
15	//!    runtime. It is called from `eval_binop` and `eval_fncall`
16	//!    only when `Environment::device()` returns `"mlx"`. The
17	//!    helper returns `Some(result)` if the named op exists in
18	//!    `mlpl-mlx-rt`, otherwise `None` so the caller can fall back to
19	//!    the CPU path.
20	//!
21	//! Triple-gate: the `mlx` Cargo feature on `mlpl-eval` pulls in
22	//! `mlpl-mlx-rt` (which itself triple-gates on
23	//! `target_os = "macos"`, `target_arch = "aarch64"`, and its own
24	//! `mlx` feature). When any of those is missing the dispatch
25	//! helper is a stub returning `None`, the `device("mlx") { }`
26	//! block falls back to CPU, and `eval_device` emits a one-time
27	//! warning so the user knows their code ran on the wrong device.
28	
29	#[cfg(all(feature = "mlx", target_os = "macos", target_arch = "aarch64"))]
30	use mlpl_array::ArrayError;
31	use mlpl_array::DenseArray;
32	use mlpl_parser::Expr;
33	use mlpl_trace::Trace;
34	
35	use crate::env::Environment;
36	use mlpl_eval_types::EvalError;
37	use mlpl_eval_types::Value;
38	
39	/// Evaluate a `device("target") { body }` block. Returns the
40	/// value of the body's last statement -- mirrors `experiment`'s
41	/// shape so a `device(...)` block is a value-yielding expression
42	/// like every other scoped form.
43	pub(crate) fn eval_device(
44	    target: &str,
45	    body: &[Expr],
46	    env: &mut Environment,
47	    trace: &mut Option<&mut Trace>,
48	) -> Result<Value, EvalError> {
49	    if let Some(dispatcher) = env.peer_dispatcher() {
50	        let source = block_source(body);
51	        let bindings = collect_array_bindings(env, &source);
52	        if let Some(result) = dispatcher.dispatch_block(target, &source, bindings) {
53	            return result;
54	        }
55	    }
56	    if !device_available(target) && env.take_device_fallback_warning() {
57	        eprintln!(
58	            "warning: device(\"{target}\") block requested but the \
59	             {target} feature is not compiled in; falling back to CPU."
60	        );
61	    }
62	    env.push_device(target.to_string());
63	    let mut last = Value::Array(DenseArray::from_scalar(0.0));
64	    for stmt in body {
65	        last = crate::eval::eval_expr(stmt, env, trace)?;
66	    }
67	    env.pop_device();
68	    Ok(last)
69	}
70	
71	fn block_source(body: &[Expr]) -> String {
72	    body.iter()
73	        .map(std::string::ToString::to_string)
74	        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
75	        .join("\n")
76	}
77	
78	fn collect_array_bindings(
79	    env: &Environment,
80	    source: &str,
81	) -> std::collections::HashMap<String, DenseArray> {
82	    env.vars_iter()
83	        .filter(|(name, _)| source.contains(name.as_str()))
84	        .map(|(name, arr)| (name.clone(), arr.clone()))
85	        .collect()
86	}

# Saga: CUDA foundation (Linux GPU backend)

## Vision

Bring real NVIDIA/CUDA GPU acceleration to sw-MLPL on Linux,
mirroring the now-complete MLX (Apple) track. The end state: a
CUDA-equivalent demo + literate `.org` doc for each MLX demo, and a
UI that connects in `?connect=` mode to an `mlpl-serve` peer running
on a Mac (MLX) AND/OR on an Arch Linux box (CUDA), gating demos by
the device the connected peer actually offers.

This first saga is the **foundation + one demo end-to-end**, proven
on real hardware. A follow-up saga mirrors the remaining MLX demos.

## Why now, why here

This dev host is an **RTX 5060 Ti (Blackwell, sm_120, 16 GB), CUDA
13.2 at `/opt/cuda`, x86_64-linux-gnu, 1.6 TB free**. Unlike the
MLX track -- which this Linux box can never build or test -- a CUDA
track is fully buildable and TDD-testable in-session with real GPU
parity tests, not Apple-only glue.

## Foundation already in place (CUDA-aware plumbing)

- **`Device::Cuda`** exists in the web-demos registry
  (`mlpl-web-demos-types`), rendered visible-but-not-runnable on the
  public live demo.
- **`Value::DeviceTensor { device: String, .. }`** already names
  `"cuda"` as a future device (`mlpl-eval-types`).
- **`device("cuda") { .. }`** already parses and pushes onto
  `Environment::device_stack`; it currently falls back to CPU with a
  one-time warning because no CUDA dispatch exists.
- **Connect mode (SSE)** routes eval to any `mlpl-serve` peer; the
  `peer_dispatcher` abstraction dispatches a whole `device(...)`
  block server-side.

## Backend decision (the analog of MLX step 005's fork)

**Chosen: `candle`** (HuggingFace `candle-core` autograd via
`Tensor::backward()` + `candle-nn` optimizers, on `cudarc`). This
mirrors the MLX track's winning "approach A": use the framework's
built-in autodiff + optimizer, zero hand-written backward formulas.
Pure Rust, no multi-GB libtorch download. The load-bearing risk is
Blackwell sm_120 / CUDA 13.2 support in `cudarc`/`candle` -- the
step-1 spike de-risks exactly that before any wider work.

Rejected: `tch` (libtorch -- heavy + Blackwell/CUDA-13 build
freshness risk) and `cudarc`-only (= MLX "approach B", ~hand-written
kernels + autodiff, explicitly rejected on the MLX track).

## Crate plan (mirror the MLX crates 1:1)

| MLX crate | Role | CUDA crate to build |
|---|---|---|
| `mlpl-mlx-rt` | forward ops | `mlpl-cuda-rt` (matmul/shape/convert) + `mlpl-cuda-elementwise` (arith) + `mlpl-cuda-nn` (activations/reductions) |
| `mlpl-mlx-forward` | embed / rms_norm / attention / cross-entropy | `mlpl-cuda-forward` |
| `mlpl-mlx-train` | autodiff + on-device Adam | `mlpl-cuda-train` |
| `mlpl-mlx-model` | `demo_forward` assembly | `mlpl-cuda-model` |
| `mlpl-mlx-serve` | server-side peer dispatcher | `mlpl-cuda-serve` |

All CUDA crates triple-gate `cfg(all(feature = "cuda", target_os =
"linux", target_arch = "x86_64"))`; absent any gate, dispatch is a
stub returning `None` and `device("cuda")` falls back to CPU with a
one-time warning (mirror `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs`).

## Steps

1. **cuda-backend-spike** -- DONE (GO). Gated crate
   `components/cuda-rt/crates/mlpl-cuda-train` proves candle's CUDA
   backend on the RTX 5060 Ti: 3 GPU tests pass (device init,
   autodiff gradient == closed-form least-squares gradient, Adam
   collapses the loss on-device). Pinned candle-core/nn 0.9.2 +
   cudarc 0.19.7 build for `sm_120` / CUDA 13.2; build incantation
   in the crate README (`CUDA_COMPUTE_CAP=120`, `/opt/cuda` env).
   candle (approach A) confirmed viable -- the rest of the saga
   proceeds on it.
2. **mlpl-cuda-rt** -- DONE. The core tensor ops split into two
   warning-free sibling crates (the eager surface is too large for
   one crate under the <=4 fn/module + <=4 module/crate budgets):
   `mlpl-cuda-rt` (convert/device plumbing, `matmul`, `reshape`,
   `transpose`) and `mlpl-cuda-elementwise` (`add`/`sub`/`mul`/`div`
   with scalar broadcast, `neg`). Both gated; 6 GPU parity tests
   pass vs the CPU path within fp32 tol. The nn surface
   (activations, softmax/reduce, `cross_entropy`) is split out to
   step 2b (`mlpl-cuda-nn`): candle lacks a `prod` reduction and
   `cross_entropy` parity is fiddly, and those ops overlap the
   step-4 candle forward.
2b. **mlpl-cuda-nn** -- DONE. The activations turned out to be
   elementwise unary maps, so they moved into `mlpl-cuda-elementwise`
   (`exp`/`log`/`relu`/`sigmoid`/`tanh` alongside `neg`, via a shared
   `unary!` macro). `mlpl-cuda-nn` is then cleanly reductions
   (`mean`/`argmax` on the GPU; `reduce_mul` delegates to the CPU --
   candle has no `prod`), normalization (`softmax`/`log_softmax`), and
   `cross_entropy` (GPU row-LSE + CPU gather, mirroring `mlpl-rt`).
   3 logic modules (reduce/norm/loss), all warning-free; parity-tested
   vs the CPU path on the GPU. Baseline held (0 new failures/warnings).
3. **cuda-dispatch-wire** -- generalize `try_mlx_dispatch` /
   `dispatched_call` in `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` so `device("cuda")`
   routes through `mlpl-cuda-rt`; CPU fallback + one-time warning
   preserved; device dispatch tests extended for cuda.
4. **cuda-forward-and-model** -- `mlpl-cuda-forward` (embed,
   rms_norm, causal_attention, cross_entropy) + `mlpl-cuda-model`
   (`demo_forward`), each parity-tested vs the CPU primitives and
   the MLX reference.
5. **cuda-lora-demo** -- `mlpl-cuda-train` (candle autodiff +
   on-device Adam) wired into `eval_adam`'s CUDA branch (analog of
   `grad_optim_mlx.rs`); first CUDA demo `demos/lora_finetune_cuda.mlpl`
   + literate `examples/literate/cuda-lora-finetune.org`; flip the
   registry entry to runnable-on-connected-CUDA-peer. Parity: the
   `device("cuda")` LoRA loss curve matches the CPU path within fp32
   tol.
6. **cuda-connect-peer** -- `mlpl-cuda-serve` so
   `mlpl-serve --features cuda` on Linux is a connect-mode peer;
   add a `GET /api/devices` capability probe so the UI knows whether
   a connected server offers `mlx`, `cuda`, or neither, and gates
   demos by the live peer instead of a static guess. This is what
   makes "connect to a Mac and/or this Arch box" honest.

## Out of scope (this saga)

- Mirroring the other 3 MLX demos (tiny_lm, neural_thicket,
  mlx_remote) + their org docs -- a FOLLOW-UP saga once the vertical
  slice is green.
- SmolLM2 loader / LLaMA-style ops (saga `local-gpu-agentic`
  Phases 4-5, now CUDA candidates -- later).
- Agentic `:ask` Phase 2/3 -- parked on `main` as
  `local-gpu-agentic` step 011, platform-agnostic, pick up on
  either host.

## References

- `docs/saga-local-gpu-agentic.md` -- the MLX track this mirrors;
  device tiers, "measurable learning" metric, demo-download policy.
- `mlpl-eval/src/device.rs` -- the single dispatch site to generalize.
- `components/native-rt/crates/mlpl-mlx-{rt,forward,train}`,
  `components/mlx-model/`, `components/serve/.../mlpl-mlx-serve` --
  the crates to mirror.
- candle: <https://github.com/huggingface/candle>;
  cudarc Blackwell/CUDA-13 support is the step-1 spike's job to pin.
